Well, one of the first things we're taught in any course that touches upon social psychology is that humans are HORRIBLE at making assumptions about systems without the data to back it up. We always think we're right but we're usually way off the mark. We tend to overvalue things like patterns or streaks without looking at the big picture. I don't mean to condescend, that's just the way it is. So the only reliable way anyone can know whether or not it's really random is through a sample, yeah. I actually think a sample like this would be relatively free of bias though, because you probably wouldn't have to control for regional differences and response bias isn't likely to be a problem unless people get salty and supply fake data. All it would really take is a reasonable number of people accurately reporting a reasonable number of maps. The only tricky part is the actual data testing. I don't want to set it up because I'm lazy and my stats is really rusty but it's absolutely feasible. Edit: Because I'm a huge nerd and I love going overboard, I did some digging to see what it would take to determine whether something is random/pseudorandom or not. Full disclosure, this is based off a few casual google searches by a person who's only taken a handful of stats courses. You can use these resources to perform your own informal sample. One of the sites suggested using a statistical test, which sounds right to me. So I found a site that automates these tests. I used a sample size of 90 because there are 9 maps and 9/90 is really easy to calculate. The "observed #" are just numbers I made up that are reasonably distributed around the expected mean of 10 occurrences per map. If the p-value you have is less than .05, then you can reasonably conclude that the results you got were unlikely to have happened by chance and therefore it's likely that the distribution of maps is NOT random. If it's GREATER than .05 then it's likely that the results ARE random. I think. Might've got that reversed. You can use an online calculator to determine the sample size you're comfortable with taking before inputting the results; the higher the sample size, the more accurate the results are likely to be. Have fun!
